GROSS ENROLMENT RATIO (GER) 
Observation/recommendation 
1. The Committee appreciates the work done by the Department in increasing the Gross 
Enrolment ratio. The Committee, however, notes that the Gross enrolment ratio of  SC/ST student 
is 23.0 and 17.2 respectively compared to the national average of 26.3. The Committee observes 
that in spite of various scholarships and initiatives taken up by the Department the GER of the 
SC/ST students has not reached to the level of nat ional average. The Committee would like to 
reiterate that the Department should take steps to bridge the gap between the general category 
students and the SC/ST students but also take initiatives so that students from these sections do not 
leave their education in between.  
(Para-3.5) 
Action Taken 
 As per AISHE Report (2018 -19) the Gross Enrolment Ratio in Higher Education – 
AllCategories-26.3, SC--23.0, ST -17.2. 
 The University Grants Commission is continuously monitoring the progress of 
implementation of reservation Policy for SCs,STs & OBC and Persons with Disabilities in 
teaching and non -teaching posts as well as admission to all level courses in universities an d 
colleges. In order to ensure that there is no discrimination against the SC/ST students, the 
Commission has notified UGC (Promotion of Equity in Higher Education Institutions) Regulation 
2012.  
 The objective of the regulations is to eliminate discrimina tion against or harassment / 
victimization of persons on the basis of their sexual orientation, gender (including the third gender) 
and also eliminate discrimination against or harassment/victimization of persons living with 
HIV/AIDS, or any other disease, physical or mental, with a stigma attached to it. These regulations 
were circulated amongst universities for implementation.  

 As a part of the effective implementation of the policy of affirmative action, UGC has 
launched a scheme to establish Equal Opportunity Cell (EOC) in institutions of higher education in 
the country. The EOCs are mandated to oversee the effective implementation of policies and 
programmes for the disadvantaged groups and to provide them guidance and counselling in 
academic, financial, social and other matters. A one -time grant of 2.00 lakhs is provided by UGC 
for establishing the office of the EOC in  universities and 75,000/- & 55,000 is respectively in UG 
and PG college.  
 Apart from EOCs, UGC supports research on the issue of social  exclusion, which has 
theoretical as well as policy importance. The centre approved in universities by UGC under the 
scheme of Centres for study of Social Exclusion and Inclusive Policy undertake following 
activities. 
 Teaching Courses at M.A and M.Phil levels, leading eventuality to full -fledged M.A and 
even M.Phil programmes in Social Exclusion Studies. 
 Undertaking M.Phil and Ph. D. supervision. 
 Undertaking empirical studies with theoretical perspective and build time series data bank 
for comparative studies and policy/programmes evaluation. 
 Carrying out detailed rigorous analyses based on the socio -economic data generated by 
government agencies. •Organizing conferences, seminars and symposia on the theme of 
Social Exclusion. 
 Publishing regularly the research findings of the faculty and students. 
 Organizing public lectures on the subject by eminent scholars. 
 Reaching out to scholars, especially young scholars, in other universities and colleges  
through an active programme of inviting Visiting Faculty. 
 Establishing links with Civil Society Organizations engaged in combating Social 
Exclusion. 
 Conducting short -term Orientation courses for political leaders, Parliamentarians, 
government officials, trade unionists and media personalities. 
 Education Quality Upgradation and Inclusion Programme (EQUIP): The EQUIP addresses 
the need to bridge the gap between SC/STs and General categories and has proposed the 
following initiatives for the same: 
 

 More financial assistantships Bridge course/ Student Induction programmes/ Career 
counselling support/ Grievance redressal of the students

Keeping in mind the fact that the field of higher education is currently facing an acute

The SAP scheme was initiated in 1963 by University Grants Commission keeping in view 
the recommendations of the Education Commission to facilitate the selected number of university 
departments having some potential in research and teaching. The program is intended to encourage 
the pursuit of excellence and teamwo rk in advanced teaching and research to accelerate the 
realization of international standards in specific fields. The first such program was initially started 
as the "Centre of Advanced Study (CAS)" in 1963. Some of these Canters also received 
recognition and financial support from UNDP/UNESCO. The "Department of Special Assistance 
(DSA)" and "Departmental Research Support (DRS)"programs were started in the Departments 
during 1972 and 1977 respectively to create feeder departments for CAS. The SAP Scheme is  
implemented at 3 levels: 
1. CENTRE OF ADVANCED STUDY (CAS) 
2. DEPARTMENT OF SPECIALASSISTANCE (DSA) 
3. DEPARTMENTAL RESEARCH SUPPORT ( DRS) The major objectives of the Special  
Assistance Program (SAP) are as follows:-  

 To identify and support university departments  that has the potential to undertake quality 
teaching and research in various educational disciplines including allied disciplines. 
 Program to be relevant to societal needs and have society and industry interaction.  
 To make research a catalyst for good teaching and introduction of new courses relating to 
identified thrust areas. 
 To have linkages with research organizations and to use their expertise innovatively to 
support research in the universities. 
 To enhance infrastructure facilities. 
 To utilize the output of research for the development of the nation and society.  
 To train and create quality human resource in identified thrust areas.  
 To search for newer / generic area(s), its promotion and nurturing. Basic Science

WOMEN EMPOWERMENT AND EDUCATION 
Observation/recommendation 
5.  The Committee observes that Higher education provided to women would mean 
independence in decision making and economic independence. It would develop capabilities to 
discharge duties and responsibilities in the fields of social, economic, political and cultural 
grounds.  
(Para-8.3) 
Action Taken 
The National Policy on Education (NPE), 1986, as revised in 1992 and further revised New 
Education Policy in 2020, a path breaking policy document, articulates the Government of Ind ia‟s 
unequivocal commitment, that “Education will be used as an agent of basic change in the status of 
women. In order to neutralize the accumulated distortions of the past, there will be a well -
conceived edge of women. This will be an act of faith and soc ial engineering…. The removal of 
women‟s illiteracy and obstacles inhibiting their services, setting time targets and effective 
monitoring…” 
It has always been a constant endeavour of the Department of Higher Education to frame 
different schemes and projects to ensure larger participation and enrolment of women.  Therefore, 
reducing the gender gap in higher education is a focus area.  There has been a phenomenal growth 
in enrolment of women students in higher education in the country. The share of girl‟s enrolment 
which was less than 10% of the total enrolment on the eve of independence has been increased to 
46.23% in the academic year 2015 -16. The GER for both Male and Female has an  increasing 
trend. The Gender gap in GER has also decreased during the period 2010 to 2015.  
Gender Budget cell is constituted with the intention of implementation and committing to 
various Gender Responsive Budgeting (GRB) initiatives with the objective o f influencing and 
effecting a change in Ministry‟s policies, programmes in a way that could tackle gender 

imbalances, promote gender equality and development and ensure that public resources through 
the Ministry budget. 
The Gender Budget Cell should compri se a cohesive group of senior/ middle level officers 
from the Plan, Policy, Coordination, Budget and Accounts Division of the Ministry concerned. 
This group should be headed by an officer not below the rank of Joint Secretary. The functions and 
working of the GRB may be reviewed at least once a quarter at the level of Secretary/ Additional 
Secretary of the Department.   
 The Gender Budget Cell in the Ministry has been re -constituted on 7th September, 2020 
with Joint Secretary (Higher Education) as Chairperson.

institutions through HEFA, the HEFA Board already has a Project Monitoring Committee 
(comprising of Directors in the HEFA Board and this Ministry‟s representa tives) that regularly 
monitors not only the expenditure of HEFA funds but also the execution of HEFA funded projects 
across educational institutions. The Dept. of Higher Education will be also putt ing in place a full -
fledged Project Monitoring Unit in the Ministry to monitor the financial and physical progress of 
all HEFA funded projects. Further, under the HEFA framework, funding for research and research 
related equipment is also provided to educa tional Institutions, apart from revenue generation 
projects. 
Further Comments of the Committee 
The Committee is not satisfied w ith the reply of the Department.  Firstly, it is 
gathered that a full-fledged Project Monitoring Unit in the Ministry to monitor the financial 
and physical progress of all HEFA funded projects  is yet to be constituted. However, no 
information or clarification has been given by the Department regarding the time period for 
constituting the Monitoring Unit. Secondly, the reply does not throw any light on the number 
of projects sanctioned/ funded under the HEFA. Further , there is no clarity as to whether  
the sanctioning / funding was given for research purpose or for procuring research related 
equipments . The Committee desires that the  Department may share the above details with 
the Committee.

OBSERVATIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS — AT A GLANCE 
 
GROSS ENROLMENT RATIO (GER) 
The Committee observes that, regardless of the umpteen numbers of schemes and 
initiatives explained, the share of enrolled SCs/STs still continue to be under -represented 
with respect to their share in the total population. As per the AISHE Report (2018 -2019) the 
highest numbers of students are  enrolled at Under Graduate level across India.   Out of the 
79.8% of the total enrolments, the Scheduled Casts students constitute only 14.9% and 
Scheduled Tribes students  constitute only 5.5% of the total  enrolment. Further, the 
percentage of SC/ST students enrolled in Post graduate programmes and Integrated 
Ph.Ds./Ph.Ds are not known.  Most of the Colleges run only Under Graduate  level 
programmes. Only 2.5% of Colleges run Ph.D. level  programmes and 34.9% of colleges run 
Post Graduate Level  programmes. Further there is a wider disparity in the GER in higher 
education in India across men and women and region wise, reflecting a significant imbalance 
within the higher education system . The Committee therefore, feels that the measures and 
schemes explained by UGC remain either underutilised or un -implemented. The Committee 
therefore proposes an outcome-based approach in higher education sector. The Committee 
may also be appraised about the status of the Revitalising  Infrastructure and Systems in 
Education (RISE) scheme which was introduced in 2018 with an aim to provide low -cost 
funds to government higher  educational institutions to expand and build new infrastructure  
and also regarding the implementation of the scheme of 10% reservation for Economically 
Weaker Section. 
 (Para-3.5)

issued after successful completion of courses online. The Committee would also like to know

difficult. The Committee feels that f aculty dearth can only be resolved if the reasons and the 
consequences are clear .  It is importa nt that the shortage of faculties in the HEIs should be 
rectified as early as possible as it may prevent education services from expanding to meet the

The Committee is of the opinion that the current system of evaluation is ineffective

REPORT 
CHAPTER – 1 
OVERVIEW OF THE DEPARTMENT 
 The Ministry of Education comprises two Departments , namely, (i) Department of 
School Education and Literacy and (ii) Department of Higher Education. The Department 
functions under the overall guidance of Minister of Education along with the Secretary, 
Department of School Education and Literacy. 
1.1 The Department  of School Education and Literacy decides the policy and 
programmes relating to school education, adult education and digital education with focus on 
quality, equity and inclusion. 
1.2 The following Institutions under the Department are involved in policy formulation 
and implementation relating to school education and adult education: 
A. National Council of Educational Research and Training(NCERT): 
1.3 The National Council of Educational Research and Training (NCERT) is an 
autonomous organisation of the Gov ernment of India : It was established on 1 st  September 
1961 as a literary, scientific and charitable Society under the Societies' Registration Act, 
1860. It provides academic and technical support for qualitative improvement in school 
education and undertakes programmes related to educational research, develo pment, training, 
international cooperation, publication and dissemination of information.  
1.4 NCERT has one national level institution, namely, National Institute of  Education, 
(NIE) New Delhi and five  Regional Institutes of Education (RIE s) located at Ajmer, Bhopal, 
Bhubaneswar, Mysuru, and Urinam (Meghalaya).  It has an institute dedicated to vocational 
studies, namely, Pandit Sunderlal Sharma Inst itute of Vocational Education, (PSSIVE), 
Bhopal and Ce ntral Institute of Educational Technology (CIET), New Delhi dedicated to 
education and technology. 
1.5 The major objectives of NCERT and its constituent units are to undertake, promote 
and coordinate research in areas related to school education; prepare a nd publish model 
textbooks, supplementary material, newsletters, journals  and develop  educational kits, 
multimedia digital materials, etc. organise pre -service and in -service training of teachers; 
develop and disseminate innovative educational techniques and practices;  collaborate and 
network with State educational departments, Universities, NGOs and other educational 
institutions; act as a clearing house for ideas and information in matters related to school 

2 
 
education; and act as a nodal agency for achieving the goals of Universalisation of 
Elementary Education. 
1.6 Among the major initiat ives taken up by NCERT are PM eVI DYA, DIKSHA - 
National Digital Infrastructure for Teachers , Manodarpan, National Initiative for School 
Heads’ and Teachers’ Holistic Advancement (NISHTHA) , Tamanna, SWAYAM Prabha TV 
Channel, Shiksha Vani on All India Radio,  
National Achievement Survey (NAS)  for class III, V, VIII and X and Development of an 
Alternative Academic Calendar during the COVID pandemic, etc.                          
B. National Council for Teacher Education (NCTE): 
1.7 The National Council for Teacher Education(NCTE) is a statutory body set up under 
the National Council for Teacher Education Act, 1993 in 1995 to formally oversee standards, 
procedures and processes in the Indian education system. This Council functions for the 
Central as well as State governments on all matter s with regard to the Teacher Education. 
NCTE seeks to bring excellence in Teacher Education programmes through planned and 
coordinated development and maintenance of standard therein. 
C. Central Board of Secondary Education (CBSE): 
1.8 The Board was given its present name ‘Central Board of Secondary Education’in 
1952. From 309 schools in 1962, the Board as of now has 24,007 schools in India and 261 
foreign countries. CBSE envisions a robust, vibrant and holistic school education that may  
engender excellence in every sphere of human endeavor. The Board is committed to provide 
quality education to promote intellectual, social and cultural vivacity among its learners. It 
works towards evolving a learning process and environment, which empowe rs the future 
citizens to become global leaders in the emerging knowledge society. The Board advocates 
and pledges to provide a stress -free learning environment that may develop competent, 
confident, and enterprising citizens who promote harmony and peace. 
                                                             
1 CBSE Affiliated schools are located in following 26 countries:  Bahrain, Bangladesh, Ethiopia, Ghana, 
Indonesia, Iran, Japan, Kenya, Kuwait, Liberia, Libya, Malaysia, Myanmar, Nepal, Nigeria, Oman, Qatar, 
Republic of Benin, Russia, Saudi Arabia, Singapore, Tansania, Thailand, Uganda, United Arab Emirates, Yemen. 

3 
 
1.9 Being an autonomous body it does not receive any funding from the Ministry of 
Education and manage from the fees collected from schools and students. Recently the CBSE 
has been entrusted with the responsibility of organizing Programme for International Student 
Assessment (PISA), 2022.  
1.10 India aims to utilize PISA as a transformative tool to further the NEP’s vision of 
transforming the school education system from rote based to competency based in order to 
empower our children to compete at the global level.  
D.  National Institute of Open Schooling (NIOS): 
1.11 National Institute of Open Schooling was set up as an autonomous organization in 
November 1989 under the Ministry of Education. NIOS is the largest open schooling system 
in the wo rld and is mandated to provide easy access to varied clientele for continuation of 
education up to pre -degree level through open and distance learning. NIOS seeks to provide 
“sustainable inclusive learning with universal and flexible access to quality scho ol education 
and skill development”. 
E. Kendriya Vidyalaya Sangathan (KVS) 
1.12 Kendriya Vidyalaya Sangathan (KVS) is an autonomous organization under the 
Ministry of Education with Headquarters at New Delhi. It was registered under the Societies’ 
Registration Act, 1860 on 15 th December, 1965. The primary aim of KVS is to  cater to the 
educational needs of the children of transferable Central Government employees including 
Defence and  Central Para -Military personnel by providing a common programme of 
education; to pursue excellence and set the pace in the field of school education; to initiate 
and promote experimentation and innovations in educati on in collaboration with other b odies 
like the Central Board of Secondary Education (CBSE) and the National  Council of 
Educational Research and Training (NCERT), etc ; and t o develop the spirit of national 
integration and create a sense of “Indianness” among children. 
1.13 The KVS (HQ) administers its schemes through 25 Regional Offices and 124 5 
Kendriya Vidyala yas including 03  at Kathmandu, Moscow and Tehran . Each Kendriya 
Vidyalaya has its Vidyalaya Management Committee headed by a senior officer from 
Defence/Civil Sector or an educationist. All the Kendriya Vidyalayas are affiliated to the 
Central Board of Sec ondary Education (CBSE), Delhi. The policies of Kendriya Vidyalaya 
Sangathan are framed through its Board of Governors headed by the Minister of Education, 
Government of India. 
 

4 
 
F. Navodaya Vidyalaya Samiti (NVS). 
1.14 Navodaya Vidyalaya Samiti (NVS) is an autonomous organization under the Ministry 
of Education and has been registered as a Society, under the Societies’ Registration Act, 1860 
at NOIDA  on 28 th February, 1986. NVS establishes, runs and manages Jawahar Navodaya 
Vidyalayas (JNVs) all over the country through its 8 Regional Offices at Bhopal, Chandigarh, 
Hyderabad, Jaipur, Lucknow, Patna, Pune and Shillong  and these schools are affiliated to 
CBSE. At present there are 661  JNVs out of which  585 are upto class X and  548 are upto 
Class XII. 
1.15 The vision of the organization is to provide good quality modern education, including 
a strong component of culture, inculcation of values, awareness of the environment, 
adventure activities and physical education, to talented children predominantly from the rural 
areas without regard to their family's socio-economic conditions. 
G. Central Tibetan Schools Administration (CTSA): 
1.16 When his Holiness the Dalai Lama along with his followers came to India in 1959, he 
showed his deep concern for education of T ibetan children in India. The then Prime Minister 
of India and His Holiness the Dalai Lama visualized the need of special schools for the 
Tibetan children and with their efforts CTSA was established in 1961. These schools mainly 
cater to the needs of Tibetan community. However, local Indian children to the extent of 10% 
are also admitted from Class VI onwards. CTSA is fully funded by Ministry of Education, 
Government of India. 
H. Directorate of Adult Education 
1.17 Directorate of Adult Education (DAE) is a subor dinate office of the Department of 
School Education & Literacy [ Ministry of Education, Government of India ]. It functions as 
the National Resource Centre for Adult Education and Literacy programmes in the country 
and provides professional, academic and tec hnical resource support and guidance for 
effective implementation of programmes launched under the aegis of the National Literacy 
Mission Authority (NLMA) from time to time. This Directorate prepares guidelines for 
development of teaching learning material , organizes training and orientation programmes, 
produces media material and harnesses all kinds of media and learner assessments. 
I. National Bal Bhavan (NBB): 
1.18 National Bal Bhavan is an autonomous body, fully funded by Ministry of Education. 
It seeks to let every child fully participate, contribute and strive towards a creative, humane, 

5 
 
innovative and joyful World in all its Wonder. The NEP, 2020 has recommended setting up 
of Bal Bhavans as special day boarding schools in States and Districts. 
J. National Education Policy, 2020 
1.19 The National Education Policy, 2020 is a basic long term policy aligned with 
aspirational goals of 21 st Century. It intends to achieve the Sustainable Development Goals 
(SDG) of the United Nations (SDG-4). With the change of name of the Ministry from Human 
Resource Development (HRD) to Ministry of Education on 18 th August, 2020 on the basis of 
suggestions c ontained in the NEP, 2020 , the policy has been  set in motion for 
implementation. The Ministry has modified existing schemes and programmes to align with 
the policy document. 
1.20  The Finance Minister on the floor of the Lok Sabha on 1 st February, 2020 has made 
announcement about 15000 exemplar schools, 100 new Sainik Schools,  750 Eklavya Model 
Residential School in tribal area  introduction of Higher Education Commission of India 
(HECI) Bill during Financial Year 2021 -22 , also amply indicates that the poli cy would be 
implemented from Financial Year 2021 -22.  The policy documents also mentions that the 
entire policy will be in operational mode during the decade 2030 -40 .This Policy will replace 
the existing Policy on Education of 1986 in phases. 
1.21 The following are the key highlights of the document:- 
 The 10+2 structure of School Curricula to be replaced with the 5+3+3+4 Curricula 
structure with five years of foundational education (upto Class 2); three years of 
preparatory stage (from Class 3 to 5); three  years of middle stage (from Class 6 to 8) 
and four years of Secondary School (from Class 9 to 12). In a nutshell, three year s of 
pre schooling/anganwadi has been proposed to be integrated with 15 years schooling 
under the NEP, 2020. 
 The Policy aims at universalization of education with 100 percent Gross Enrolment 
Ratio (GER) by  the year 2030 for school education and 50 percent by  the year 2035 
for higher education. 
 3.22 crore out of school children in the age group of 6 to 17 years to be brought back 
school to achieve 100% GER by the year 2030. 
 Additional Kendriya Vidyalayas (KVs) and Navodaya Vidyalayas (NVs) to be set up 
in aspirational districts and Special Education Zone (SEZ). 
 National Mission of Foundational Literacy and Numeracy (NMFLN) for attain ing 
universal foundational literacy and numeracy in all primary schools for all learners by 
Grade three by the year 2025. 
 National Curricular and Pedagogical Framework for Early Childhood Care and 
Education (NCPFECCE) for children upto the age of eight to be developed by the 
NCERT.  
 A Comprehensive National Curriculum Framework for Teachers Education (NCFTE) 
will be formulated by National Council for Teachers Education (NCTE) in 
consultation with NCERT, by the year 2021.  
 

6 
 
 Three language formula in school e ducation; mother tongue/regional or local 
language to be used as a medium of i nstitution till Grade Five and m ay be extended 
till Grade Eight and beyond.  
 Performance Assessment, Review and Analysis of Knowledge for Holistic 
Development (PARAKH) to be set up as a standard setting body at national level; 
States to develop State School Standard Authority (SSSAs) and the SCERT to 
develop School Quality Assessment and Accreditation Framework (SQAAF).  
 A common National Professional Standard for Teachers (NPST) to be developed by 
National Council for Teachers Education (NCET) in consultation with NCERT and 
SCERT. 
 National Research Foundation (NRF) to set up as an apex body to foster research and 
innovation culture and to build research capacity across higher educ ation (both public 
and private).  
 Universities and Colleges to bloom into full fledged research centre of excellence 
with support and guidance of NRF. 
 An Academic Bank to Credit to be set up for digitally storing academic credit earned 
from different Highe r Education Institutions (HEIs) and can be transferred and 
counted towards final degree earned.   
 Higher Education Commission of India (HECI) to be set up as an overarching 
umbrella body of higher education excluding medical and legal education. 
 The Higher Education Commission of India will have independent bodies i.e. 
National Higher Education Regulatory Council (NHERC) and General Education 
Council (GEC) for regulation; Higher Education Grant Council (HEGC) for funding 
and financing and National  Assessment and Accreditation Council (NAAC) for 
accreditation. 
 A National Mission for Mentoring to be set up with a large pool of outstanding 
senior/retired faculty to provide longterm mentoring/professional support to 
university/college teachers.  
 Bal Bhawans as special day boarding schools to be set up in States and Districts. 
 Gender Inclusion Fund (GIF) for equitable and quality education for all girl children 
and transgender and Special Education Zones (SEZ) for disadvantaged regions and 
groups.  
 Integration of Vocational Education with mainstream education  from primary to 
university level in a phased manner ; vocational education/internship from Class 6 
onwards.  
 Vocational Educational is received by 5% of youth in India in contradiction to 52% in  
USSR, 75% in Germany and 96% in South Korea. Policy lays emphasis to raise it to 
50% by 2025.  
 Holistic Education by removing distinction between Curricula, Co -Curricular and 
Extracurricular activities.  
 Standardized State School Examination for Grade 3, 5 and 8 and Board Exams for 
Grade 10 and 12.  
 Centre and States to work to increase public investment in education to reach six 
percent of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) or twenty percent of public expenditure. 
 Multidisplinary Education and Research Universities ( MERUs) (with enrollment in  
thousands) at par with IIT and IIM to be set up in each nearby districts with Education 
Department offering four year multi disciplinary B.Ed Programme for quality 
teachers, by the year 2030.  
 Indian Institution of Translation and Interpretation (IITI) to be set up. 
 National Institute(s) for Pali, Prakrit and Persian to be set up. 
 

7 
 
 Entering of top world rank universities to open campus in our country for 
internationalization of education. 
 Four Year Integrated B.Ed would be minimum requirement for teaching in schools by 
the year 2030.  
 National Education Teaching Forum (NFTF) will be created as a full fledged  
organisation for free exchange of ideas on use of technologies or to enhance learning, 
assessment and administration.  
 National Institute of Open Schooling (NIOS) to develop modules for sign languages 
for special need children. 
 National Testing Agency (NTA) to conduct entrance tests for admission  to Higher 
Education Institutions.  
 Holistic Multidisciplinary Education with mult iple entry/exit options for higher 
education.  
 Equitable and Inclusive Education with special focus on Social Economical 
Disadvantaged Groups (SEDGs).  
 Open Distance Learning (ODL) offered by NIOS and State Open Schools to be used 
to increase GDR.  
 Skill L abs to be created on hub spoke model with ITI, Polytechnics and local 
industries for vocational education; students should learn Lok vidya (Soft-skill).  
 Emphasis on Research and Innovation , which is 0.69% of GDP in our coun try as 
compared to 2.8% in USA, 4.3% in Israel and 4.2% in South Korea, etc. and increase 
investment on research and innovation.  
 Indian Council for Agricultural Research (ICAR), Veterinary Council of India (VCI), 
Council of Architecture (COA), National Cou ncil for Teachers Education (NCTE), 
National Council for Vocational Education and Training (NCVET) will act as 
Professional Standard Setting Bodies (PSSBs). 
 M.Phil Degree to be abolished, four year multidisciplinary graduate could pursue 
doctoral research with or without post graduate degree.  
 Planning and implementation of ECCE will be jointly carried out by Ministry of 
Education, Ministry of Women and Child Development, World and Tribal Affairs.  
 Pupil Teacher Ratio (PTR) ,i.e., 30:1, mentioned in RTE Act 2009 to be ensured at all 
level in school.  
 In addition to Indian languages and English, foreign languages ,i.e., Korean, Japanese, 
Thai, French, German, Portuguese and Russian will be offered at Secondary Level.  
 National Curriculum Framework for School Education (NCFSE) 2020 -21 will be 
prepared by NCERT on the basis of NEP 2020 and will be made available in all 
regional languages and to be updated periodically in every 5 to 10 years.  
 100 tourist destinations will be identified and school children will b e taken to some of 
those destinations to understand and appreciate diversity, culture and tradition of our 
country under ‘Ek Bharat Shreshta Bharat’.  
 Creation of Children Library, On Line Library, Social Book Hubs, Digital Library and 
National Book Promotion Policy for generating reading habits among the children.  
 Bilingual Education for future Lawyers and Judges in Law Universities.  
 Ensuring Universal access to ECCE to children by, 2030 as nearly 5 crore children 
have not attained foundational literacy and numeracy resulting in learning crisis in the 
educational system. 
 Teaching material and methodology to be enquiry -based, discussion - based, 
discovery-based and analysis-based rather than depending on rote learning.

1.22 The Department of School Education and Literacy in their clarification submitted to 
the Committee in the meeting held on 5th March 2021 informed about the steps taken for 
implementation of NEP, 2020 as follows:- 
1.23 A total 180 Paras of NEP recommendations relate to School Education including 12 
common Paras for both School Education and Higher Education, 36 Paras are common for 
National Curriculum Framework (NCF) and Samagra Shiksha, 52 Paras to be covered under 
NCF, 45 Paras are directly related to Samagra Shiksha scheme, 1 Para to be covered under 
MDM scheme, 5 Paras covered by Padhna Likhna Abhiyan, 41 Par as to be implemented by 
various autonomous bodies/Ministries/states/UTs/guidelines/etc. 
 86 Paras of NEP have been covered/integrated under the scheme of 
SamagraShiksha which include: Introduction of 1 year of Balvatika and TLMs to all 
children, National Mission of Foundational Literacy and Numeracy, Holistic Progress 
Card (HPC), Introduction of tracking of learning outcomes as well as transition of 
children, Induction of qualified counsellors at secondary and senior secondary level in 
a phased manner, Language Teachers, Capacity building of teachers (50 Hrs CPD), 
Bagless days and internships, Support for OOSC in age group of 16 - 19 years, 
Activities of PARAKH, Separate stipend for C WSN girl child; provision for 
identification of CWSN and Resource Centre at block level, expansion of schooling 
facilities including Residential Hostels, KGBVs etc., Provision for Hub and Spoke 
model in vocational education, Provision for Smart classroom a nd support for 
DIKSHA, Support for Assessment Cells in SCERT etc.  
 Theme/component specific Goals and Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) have been 
developed to monitor the progress on time to time.  
 Similarly, Mid Day Meal (MDM) and Adult Education Schemes of the department 
are being aligned with the NEP 2020.

L.  Samagra Shiksha (Centrally Sponsored Scheme): 
1.27 Samagra Shiksha , an overarching programme for the school education sector 
extending from pre -school to class 12, is being implemented with the broader goal of 
improving school effectiveness measured in terms of equal opportunities for schooling and 
equitable learning out comes. The vision of the Scheme is to ensure inclusive and equitable 
quality education from pre -school to senior secondary stage in accordance with the 
Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) for Education. The main outcomes of the Scheme are 
envisaged as Universal Access, Equity and Quality including Vocational Education, Inclusive 
Education, increased use of Technology and strengthening of Teacher Education Institutions 
(TEIs) and treat school education holistically as a continuum from Pre-school to Class 12. 
M. Strengthening Teaching-Learning and Results for States (STARS):  
1.28 STARS is an externally aided project (supported by World Bank) which will be 
implemented as a Centrally Sponsored Scheme.  The total cost of the project is approximately 
₹ 5718 Crore, with US$ 500 million (approximately ₹. 3700 Crore) to be funded by the 
World Bank and rest coming as State share from the participating States. The project covers 6 
States, viz., Himachal Pradesh, Rajasthan, Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, Kerala and Odisha. 
The identified States will be supported for various interventions for improving the quality of 
education. 
N. National Programme of Mid-Day Meal in Schools (MDM): 
1.29 The National Programme of Mid -Day Meal in Schools, popularly known as the Mid -
Day Meal Scheme, is an on -going Centrally -Sponsored Scheme which covers all school 
children studying in Classes I -VIII of Government, Government -Aided, Special Training 
Centres including Madarsas and Maqtabs supported under Samagra Shiksha. During 2019-
20, 11.80 crore children studying in 11.20 lakh institutions have been benefitted under the 
Scheme. The NEP,2020 have also advocated introduction of breakfast under the scheme. 
O. National Means-cum-Merit Scholarship Scheme (NMMSS): 
1.30 The Central Sector Scheme, ‘National Means -cum-Merit Scholarship Scheme’, was 
launched in May, 2008 with the objective to award scholarships to meritorious students of 
economically weaker sections @ ₹6000/- per annum (₹500/- per month) per student to arrest 
their dropout at Class VIII and encourage them to continue the ir studies at secondary stage. 
The rate of scholarship has been enhanced from ₹6000/ - to ₹12000/ - per year with effect 
from 1st April, 2017. 
 

11 
 
 
P. Padhna Likhna Abhiyan 
1.31 A new scheme of adult education , namely; Padhna Likhna Abhiyan , has been 
launched for implementation during the FY 2020 -21. The main objective and thrust of the 
scheme is on basic literacy, i.e., on making illiterate adults literate. The scheme has a flexible 
approach and innovative methodologies such as involving school and college stude nts and 
other volunteers of Schemes, such as, National Cadet Corps (NCC), National Service Scheme 
(NSS) and Nehru Yuva Kendra Sangathan (NYKS), for imparting basic literacy.

Implementation of the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009 
3.12 The Committee was apprised that our country is one  of the 135 countries which has  
made education a fundamental right. With the enactment of the Right of Children to Free and 
Compulsory Education Act, 2009 (also known as RTE, Act) education has been included 
under Article – 21A of Constitution. With its enactment of the RTE Act, children in the age 
group of 6 to 14  and Classes 1 to 8  have been provided free and compulsory education. The 
education for them is compulsory as the RTE Act cast an obligation on appropriate 
Government to ensure admi ssion, attendance and completion of education by all children 
between 6 to 14 age group leaving no child behind. It was also free in the sense that children 
are not required to pay any fee/charges/expenses which may prevent him/her to pursue 
elementary education. Free uniform, books have been provided to children. The said Act also 
reserves 25% seats for Children from Economically Weaker Section for  ensuring equitable 
education. 
3.13 The Committee noted that since NEP  lays down  Curricula Structure 5 +3+3+4, the 
child would be in the school from age of 3 and amendment to RTE Act could be necessitated 
to provide free and compulsory education to children from the age of 3 which is now from 
the age of 6.  The Department  accordingly may ensure that the children of age group of 6 to 
14 years entitled for free and compulsory education  under the RTE Act  may be changed to 
age group of 3 to 14 years to implement the NEP, 2020.

No Detention Policy and National Achievement Survey 
3.15 The RTE Act mandates that no students will be detained upto Class 8. A system of 
Comprehensive and Continuous Evaluation (CCE) was introduced for performance 
assessment but that was not effectively monitored due to which high failure and dropouts in 
Classes 9 and 10 were observed. More so, many students do not focus much on education as 
they already have a mindset that they would be promoted to the next class even if they don’t 
perform well. Some states were against the policy and some other states were in favour of the 
policy. It was also felt that the policy would leave a negative impact on the standard of 
education in India.  
3.16 The Committee in its Three Hundredth Report had endorsed the amendment proposed 
to the RTE Act and States had been given the option to decide retention or scrapping of the 
non-retention policy. To the query as to what is the impact of amendments to the RTE Act to 
give option to State Governments to decide about retention or scrapping of no detention 
policy, the Department has not got feed backs from the States due to pandemic.  
3.17 The Committee was informed that  NCERT conducted National Achievement Survey 
(NAS) in 2017 to assess the competencies developed by the children at the grade level III, V 
and VIII in different subject areas such as languages, mathematics, EVS/Science and Social 
Science in Government and Government aided schools.  It was done in 701 distri cts in 36 
States and UTs. It covered 22 lakh students and 1.10 lakh schools ; and for class X it covered 
15 lakh students and 4430 schools across 610 districts in 34 States/UTs. The findings of the  
survey indicates poor learning outcome of the children.  
3.18 The Secretary, Department of School Education and Literacy in her submissions 
before the Committee on 5 th March, 2021 informed that NAS 2020 has been postponed to 
NAs 2021 due to Covid and will be conducted on 12 th November, 2021. She informed the 
distinction between methodology of survey conducted through National Achievement Survey 
(NAS) and Annual Status of Education Report (ASER) as follows:- 
i. NAS is under Samagra Shiksha while the States governments can conduct  States 
Achievement Survey (SAS); 
ii. NAS is paper based test to assess the learning achievements of the students in certain 
subjects while ASER is a household survey to test learning deficiency; 
iii. NAS average achievement of Class III students in language is 68%, whereas ASER 
shows that 27.2% class III children can read class II level text;  

29 
 
iv. NAS average achievement of students of Class III in Mathematics is 64% whereas 
ASER reports that class III children in govt. schools who can atleast do subtraction is 
20.9%; 
v. NAS, average achievement of Class VIII students in language is 57% where is ASER 
reports that 27%  class VIII children can’t read; and  
vi. NAS, average achievement of class VIII students in Mathematics is 42% whereas 
ASER reports that 56% students of class VIII can’t do basic Mathematics. 
 
3.19 The Committee was informed that the competency based test was based on the 
Learning Outcomes which were recently incorporated in the Central Rules framed under the 
RTE Act, 2009. 
3.20 The Committee  is happy to note that concept of learning outcome has b een 
recognized under the rules under RTE Act and expresses its satisfaction over the 
methodology used to assess learning competency of students at Class III, V, VIII, X. 
3.21 The Committee took note that RTE Act prior to its amendment in 2019 had No -

monitored by the respective Schools. The NAS introduced in 2017 by NCERT is an effective

Vacancies Across Organizations Under The Department: 
 3.32 Members raised concern about the status of vacancies in the organizations under the 
department. The Committee noted that in KVS a total of 13949 vacancies exist out o f which 
5991 were of teachers (both  TGT & PGT ) as on 31 st December, 2020 out of the teachers 
vacancies 587 are of EWS category, 1611 are of OBC category, 898 are of SC category, 450 
are of ST category, 165 are of PWD category. Likewise, 3407 vacancies exist in NVS out of 
which 671 are of OBC category, 414 are of  SC category, 351 are of ST category and 176 are 
of PWD category. In CBSE 92 9 vacancies (out of 1833) exist;  in NCERT 16 44 vacancies 
(out of 2833); i n NIOS 171 vacancies (out of 394)  and in CTSA 130 vacancies (out of 318) 
exist.  
3.33 The Committee notes t hat the vacancies of teachers tend to affect the teacher pupil 
ratio in schools and also creates extra burden on the existing teachers. The  procedure of 
appointment of  contractual teachers tend s to violate the reservation policy of the 
Government. The State is duty bound to ensure reservation in appointment of post under the 
Government.  
3.34 The Committee expresse s its concern over the status of vacancies and 
recommends that a special time bound recruitment drive should be conducted to fill all 
the existing vacancies, as contractual teachers/staff are always likely to have a sense of 
insecurity due to temporary nature of job besides giving a wrong impression about the 
Government’s commitment for social Justice.

National Education Policy, 2020 
3.57 The National Education Policy way back in 1968 had emphasized upon public 
expenditure of 6% (by both Centre and States) of the Gross Domestic Product (GDP) , which 
has been reiterated in Education Policy of 1986 and reaffirmed by the NEP of 2020. But the 
current expenditure of Government at Union and States is around 4% of Gross Domestic 
Product (GDP) , which is roughly 10% of  the total Government expenditure. Among the 
SAARC Countries, Nepal and Bhutan spent more than India on their Education. 
3.58 The corresponding figures stand at 7.5 percent 3 for Bhutan, Zimbabwe and Sweden; 7 
percent for Costa Rica and Finland; 6 percent for Kyrgyzstan, South Africa and Bra zil; 5.5 
percent for United Kingdom, Netherlands and Palestine; and 5 percent for Malaysia, Kenya, 
Mongolia, Korea and United States of America. 
3.59 The Committee has been apprised that a total of ₹ 93224.00 crore has been allocated 
for Ministry of Education for Financial Year 2021 -22 with 58.86 percent for Department of 
School Education and Literacy and 41.14 percent for Department of Higher Education, which 
comes to around 2.29 percent of  the total budgetary allocation by the Union  Government to 
all its Ministries/Departments. The budgetary allocations on Sainik Schools which comes

99 are made to Ministry of Defence and Ministry of Tribal Affairs, resp ectively. The

Social Justice and Empowerment , while merit -cum-means scholarship is under the 
Department of School Education and Literacy. So factoring  in all allocations for the purpose 
of education largely remains around 3 percent of Union Budget. As noted in NEP, 2020, 6% 
of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) or 20% of public expenditure is required annually to 
achieve the target set in education policy. As of now, all States , together spent 75 to 80% 
while the Union Government spent around 20 to 25% of its total expenditure on education  
which is  around 4% of the GDP . Accordingly, the Committee recommends that the 
Department should take  more proactive measures to bring the S tates and UTs in 
alignment with the schemes and programmes of the Government of India so that the 
total expenditure on Education as a whole can be projected accurately. 
Pre Schooling Education 
3.60 The Committee was apprised that the 10+2 structure of school curricula is to be 
replaced with a 5+3+3+4 curricula structure with 5 years of foundational education (upto 
Class 2); three years of preparatory stage (from Class 3 to 5); three year s of middle stage 
(from Class 6 to 8) and four years of Secondary S chool from Class 9 to 12. First five years of 
foundational learning entails three years period at Anganwadi/Bal Vatika , which is proposed 
to be clubbed with first two grades of schooling. The State wise Specific Attendance Ratio 
(ASAR) for t he year (2017 -18) referred to in  Economic Survey (2020 -21) at Page 331 was 
brought to the notice of the Committee wherein attendance in the age group of 3 to 5 years 
(Early Childhood Education) at national level is 33.1% with Punjab having high est 
attendance and Karnatak a with the lowest attendance rate. The National Education Policy 
(NEP), 2020 has proposed for inclusion of pre- schooling in the school curricula. 
3.61 The Committee is happy to note that Early Childhood Care and Education (ECCE) 
has been proposed to be introduced in public schools which has been followed by some of the 
private schools in the form of play school and nursery. It is widely accepted that during this 
age, 85% of cumulative development of brain takes place , which has definitive bearing on 
acquisition of knowledge and skill s in later life.  The Committee recommends that as 
envisaged in NEP, 2020 the preparation of National Curricula and Pedagogical 
Framework for Early Childhood Care and Education (NCPFECCE) for children upto 8 
years of age should  be done on priority basis with due seriousness so as to ensure it’s 
early and effective implementation.

Director, National Bal Bhavan (NBB) and Directorate of Adult Education made power point 
presentation explaining details of activities under taken by their respective bodies.

for Mid-day Meal Scheme; vacancies in various bodies under the Department; time frame for 
strengthening 15,000 schools as exemplar schools; the Natio nal Digital Education 
Architecture; gross enrolment ratio time frame by which all aspirational districts will have a 
Central School; and reasons for the reduction in funds for the National Scheme for Incentive 
to Girl Child for Secondary Education; on key performance matrics for KVS, NVS, NIOS. 
Issues relating to 360 degree assessment of teachers; transparency in the admission process in 
KVS under the discretionary quota; optimal utilization of the infrastructure available to the 
KVs; steps taken to check s chool drop -outs; streamlining of CBSE affiliation process; and 
setting up of Regional Institutes of Education of NCERT at various places for quality teacher 
education.

during CO VID-19 pandemic and lockdown particularly from students belonging to EWS 
category and posed query as to whether the Department was taking any steps for the capacity 
building of non- teaching staff; details of the co -ordination mechanism between the differe nt 
organizations of the Department; Fund allocation to KGBVs and steps taken to fill up the 
vacancies in the organization concerned.

OVERVIEW OF THE MINISTRY 
INTRODUCTION  
 
1.0 Ministry of Education (Shiksha Mantralaya) comprises of two Departments:  
 i) Department of School Education & Literacy (SE & L) ;and  
            ii) Department of Higher Education (HE)  
 
1.1 The Department of Higher Education, Ministry of Education, is responsible for the 
overall development of the basic infrastructure of Higher Education sector, both in terms of 
policy and planning.  
1.2  The Department of Higher Education has  the  visio n to realize India’s human 
resource potential to its fullest in the higher education sector with equity and excellence. 
Department of Higher Education has the following mission: 
 Provide greater opportunities of access to higher education with equity to all  the 
eligible persons and in particular to the vulnerable sections. 
 Initiate policies and programmes for strengthening research and innovations and 
encourage institutions – public or private – to engage in stretching the frontiers of 
knowledge. 
 Promote the  quality of higher education by investing in infrastructure and faculty, 
promoting academic reforms, improving governance and institutional restructuring 
towards the inclusion of the hitherto deprived communities. 
1.3   The Department of Higher Education has the  following  objectives: 
 To increase the Gross  Enrolment Ratio (GER) in Higher Education; 
 To create and expand institutional base of higher education with involvement of  State 
 Governments and Non-Governmental Organizations/civil society. 
 To provid e opportunities to socially -deprived communities including women, 
 minorities and differently-abled persons. 
 To remove regional imbalances by se tting up of institutions in aspirational  districts 
 and  special education zones 
 To enhance support for infrastructure and faculty development in higher education 
 institution . 
 To create conditions for knowledge generation through improved research facilities in 
 universities and colleges. 

2 
 
 To promote collaboration with International c ommunity, foreign governments, 
 universities/institutions and regional and international institutions, for the 
 advancement of universal knowledge and intellectual property rights. 
 To promote development of Indian languages. 
 To promote autonomy and  academic reforms in institutions of higher learning 
1.4    The Department of Higher Education   has the  following apex  level bodies: 
a)   University Grant Commission (UGC), New Delhi;   
  The University Grants Commission (UGC) is a Statutory Body established by 
an Act of Parliament in 1956 for the promotion and coordination of University 
Education and for the determination and maintenance of standards of teaching, 
examination and research in Universities. Apart from providing grants to Universities 
and college s, the Commission takes measures necessary for development of higher 
education. The UGC functions from its Headquarter at New Delhi and its six Regional 
Offices located at Hyderabad, Pune, Bhopal, Kolkata, Guwahati, Bengaluru and 
Northern Regional College Bureau in Delhi 
b)   All India Council for Technical Education (AICTE), New Delhi; 
  All India Council for Technical Education (AICTE)  submitted  that AICTE 
was set -up in November 1945 as national level Apex Advisory Body to conduct 
survey on the faciliti es on technical education and to promote development in the 
country in a coordinated and integrated manner.  
c)   Council of Architecture, New Delhi; 
   CoA was established on 31st December, 1976 under Architect Act,  
 1972. It maintains register of architects and recommends the recognition of Indian as 
 well as foreign architectural degree. It conducts NATA for admission in 5 year    
 B.Arch 
d)   National Testing Agency New Delhi 
  The NTA is an independent autonomous and self -sustained premier 
 organization  registered under Societies Regulation Act, 1860 on 15 May, 
 2018 as a self- reliant and  self sustained premier testing organization. The NEP, 
 2020 mandates all the entrance exams for admission into HEI to be conducted by 
 NTA.

INDIAN COUNCIL OF SOCIAL SCIENCE RESEARCH (ICSSR), NEW DELHI 
1.6 Indian Council of Social Science Research (ICSSR) was established in the year 1969 
by the Government of India to promote research in social sciences in the country and apex 
social science research body fully funded by the Government of India). ICSSR funds research 
to the faculties/scholars in universities, research institutes, institutes of national importance 
and colleges.  
1.7    The ICSSR provides maintenances and dev elopment grants to Research Institutes and 
fully funds its Regional Centres located in different parts of the country. The council is at 
present supporting 24 Research institutes, 6 Regional Centres & 5 Recognized Institutes. The 
Council has already publis hed, in addition to journals, a large number of books and 
monographs on issues of vital importance. It also publishes survey of research in different 
social science disciplines such as Economics, Political Science, Sociology and Social 
Anthropology, Psychology, and Geography. 
 
INDIAN COUNCIL OF HISTORICAL RESEARCH (ICHR)  
1.8 Indian Council of Historical of Research (ICHR) is an autonomous organization 
which was established under Societies Registration Act (Act XXI of 1860) in 1972. The 
prime objectives of the Council are to give a proper direction to historical research and to  
encourage and foster objective and scientific writing of history. The broad aims of the 
Council are to bring historians together, provide a forum for exchange of views between 
them, give a national direction to an objective and rational presentation inter pretation of 
history, to sponsor historical research programmes and projects and to assist institutions and 
organizations engaged in historical research. It has a broad view of history so as to include in 
its fold the history of Science and Technology, Eco nomy, Art, Literature, Philosophy, 
Epigraphy, Numismatics, Archaeology, Socio - Economic formation processes and allied 
subjects containing strong historical bias and contents.

NEW EDUCATION POLICY,2020 
1.18 The Department of  Higher   Education  in its submission before the Committee on 
NEP-2020 highlighted that this was the first education policy of the 21st century and aims 
revamp  all aspects of the education structure including regulation and governance to create a 
new system aligned with the aspirational goals of 21st century education while building upon 
India's tradition and value systems. 
1.19  The following are the  key highlights of the document relating to Higher  Education:-   
 Increase GER to 50 % by 2035 
 NEP 2020 aims to increase the Gross Enrolment Ratio in higher education including 
vocational education from 26.3% (2018) to 50% by 2035. 3.5 Crore new seats will be 
added to Higher education institutions. 
 The policy envisages broad based, multi -disciplinary, holistic Under Graduate 
education with flexible curricula, creative combinations of subjects, integration of 
vocational education and multiple entry and exit points wit h appropriate certification. 
UG education can be of 3 or 4 years with multiple exit options and appropriate 
certification within this period. For example, Certificate after 1 year, Advanced 
Diploma after 2 years, Bachelor’s Degree after 3 years and Bachelo r’s with Research 
after 4 years. 
 An Academic Bank of Credit is to be established for digitally storing academic credits 
earned from different HEIs so that these can be transferred and counted towards final 
degree earned. 
 Multidisciplinary Education and Res earch Universities (MERUs), at par with IITs, 
IIMs, to be set up as models of best multidisciplinary education of global standards in 
the country. 
 The National Research Foundation will be created as an apex body for fostering a 
strong research culture and building research capacity across higher education. 
 Higher Education Commission of India(HECI) will be set up as a single overarching 
umbrella body the for entire higher education, excluding medical and legal education. 
HECI to have  four independent verti cals  - National Higher Education Regulatory 
Council (NHERC) for regulation, General Education Council (GEC ) for standard 
setting, Higher Education Grants Council (HEGC) for funding,  and National 
Accreditation Council( NAC) for accreditation. HECI will f unction through faceless 
intervention through technology, & will have powers to penalise HEIs not conforming 
to norms and standards. Public and private higher education institutions will be 

7 
 
governed by the same set of norms for regulation, accreditation an d academic 
standards. 
 Higher education institutions will be transformed into large, well resourced, vibrant 
multidisciplinary institutions providing high quality teaching, research, and 
community engagement. The definition of university will allow a spectr um of 
institutions that range from Research -intensive Universities to Teaching -intensive 
Universities and Autonomous degree-granting Colleges.  
 Affiliation of colleges is to be phased out in 15 years and a stage -wise mechanism is 
to be established for granting graded autonomy to colleges. Over a period of time, it is 
envisaged that every college would develop into either an Autonomous degree -
granting College, or a constituent college of a university. 
 NEP makes recommendations for motivating, energizing,  and building capacity of  
faculty through  clearly defined, independent, transparent recruitment , freedom to 
design curricula/pedagogy, incentivizing excellence, movement into institutional 
leadership. Faculty not delivering on basic norms will be held accountable 
 Open and Distance Learning 
 This will be expanded to play a significant role in increasing GER. Measures such as 
online courses and digital repositories, funding for research, improved student 
services, credit-based recognition of MOOCs, etc., wi ll be taken to ensure it is at par 
with the highest quality in-class programmes. 
 Online Education and Digital Education: 
 A comprehensive set of recommendations for promoting online education consequent 
to the recent rise in epidemics and pandemics in order  to ensure preparedness with 
alternative modes of quality education whenever and wherever traditional and in -
person modes of education are not possible, has been covered. A dedicated unit for 
the purpose of orchestrating the building of digital infrastruct ure, digital content and 
capacity building will be created in the MHRD to look after the e -education needs of 
both school and higher education. 
 Technology in education 
 An autonomous body, the  National Educational Technology Forum (NETF),  will 
enhance learn ing, assessment, planning, administration. Appropriate integration of 
technology into all levels of education will be done to improve classroom processes, 
support teacher professional development, enhance educational access for 
disadvantaged groups and str eamline educational planning, administration and 
management 
 Promotion of Indian languages 
 To ensure the preservation, growth, and vibrancy of all Indian languages, NEP 
recommends setting an  Indian Institute of Translation and Interpretation 
(IITI), National Institute (or Institutes) for Pali, Persian and Prakrit , 
strengthening of Sanskrit and all language departments in HEIs,   and use mother 
tongue/local language as a medium of instruction in more HEI  programmes . 

8 
 
 Internationalization of education will be facilitated through both institutional 
collaborations, and student and faculty mobility and allowing entry of top world 
ranked Universities to open campuses in our country. 
 Professional Education 
 All professional education will be an integral part of the h igher education system. 
Stand-alone technical universities, health science universities, legal and agricultural 
universities etc will aim to become multi-disciplinary institution

and Women in Higher  Educational  Institutions including Institutes of National 
Importance, Deemed Universities funded by Central Government. 
NATIONAL EDUCATION POLICY ,2020  
3.7 National Education Policy (NEP), 2020  envisages an  overarching framework to promote 
Research and Innovation under  the Principal Scientific Advisor (PSA) in consultation with NITI 
Aagog. The scheme was also announced in Budget 2019 and Prime Minister’s Independence Day 
2020 speech. The proposed NRF, according to th e NEP, aims to enable a culture of research in 
higher education institutions through competitive funding across disciplines . 
3.8  The Committee recommends that t he funding from National Research 
Foundation(NRF) and fellowships/scholarships should focus on   themes having national 
importance as  identified after due consultations with diff erent 
 Ministries/organizations. 
GLOBAL  INITIATIVE FOR ACADEMIC NETWORK (GIAN) 
3.9 Global Initiative of Academic Networks (GIAN) in Higher Education was launched 
on 30th N ovember, 2015. The programme seeks to invite distinguished academicians, 
entrepreneurs, scientists, experts from premier institutions from across the world, to teach in 
the higher educational institutions in India . The Scheme envisages garnering the best 

20 
 
international experience into our systems of education, enabling interaction of students and 
faculty with the best academic and industry experts from all over the world.  
3.10 Internationally reputed academicians from all over the world were invited primarily to 
teach in the Higher Educational Institutes (HEIs) of India and to initiate teaching and research 
collaborations. IIT Kharagpur is the national coordinating institute for GIAN and Director IIT 
Kharagpur is the National Coordinator for GIAN Scheme. 
3.11 The Department in its submission before the Committee informed that  GIAN Scheme 
is proposed to be modified as GIAN plus. In the existing GIAN scheme, there is a provision 
for one-way interaction i.e., foreign faculties are coming to India to teach in I ndian Academic 
Institutions. The Expert Committee constituted by the Ministry recommended that the 
existing GIAN initiative need to be re -modeled and named as GIAN Plus by making a 
provision for Indian faculties to teach in reputed foreign institutions. Th is way, in the GIAN 
Plus, two-way interaction has been proposed b y sending good Indian faculty abroad which 
would provide them exposure to best international practices, so that they  can come back and 
create a more permanent positive change in the practices being followed in their universities 
by improving content, instructional design, delivery, assessment and course Management 
skills. The Department submitted that a total of 1585 nu mber of foreign faculties have taught 
in different Higher Education Institutions (HEI) in India both in private and government 
institutions.  
3.12 The Committee recommends that the Department should also strengthen the 
'Study in India' scheme and advertise  it  in other countries  especially in South east 
Asian, African, Central Asian  and Latin American countries for a faculty exchange 
program and awarding double  diploma/degree to the students availing this Scheme. It 
is advised that the recommendations of  the Destination India Conference held in Pune 
in January 2020 on the subject of Making India a Hub of Higher Education be taken 
into consideration seriously.    
SCHOLARSHIP  SCHEMES 
CENTRAL SECTOR SCHEME OF SCHOLARSHIP  (CSSS) FOR COLLEGE AND 
UNIVERSITY STUDENTS 
3.13 The objective of the scheme is to provide financial assistance for meeting day to day 
expenses while pursuing higher education, to meritorious students having family income of 

21 
 
less than ₹ 8 lakhs per annum.  The total number of scholarships is 82000 (41000 for boys 
and 41000 for girls). Students who are in top 20th percentile of successful candidates in the 
relevant stream from a particular Board of Examination in class,  pursuing regular course and 
ot availing of any other scholarship scheme, are eligible for consideration under this Scheme. 
The rate of scholarship is ₹10,000/- per annum for the first three years and ₹. 20,000/- per 
annum for the fourth and fifth year. Scholarship amount i s disbursed directly into the bank 
account of the beneficiaries through Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) mode w.e.f. 1.1.2013. 
The scheme has on -boarded the National Scholarship portal (NSP) www.scholarships.gov.in 
with effect from 1.8.2015. Students belongin g to reserved categories/weaker sections 
/minorities are eligible on the basis of merit, subject to Central Reservation Policy. 
Reservations for the various categories are as follows: Scheduled Castes (SCs) 15 %, 
Scheduled Tribes (STs) 7.5 %, Other Backwar d Classes (OBCs) 27 % and horizontally 5% 
for Persons(s) with Disabilities (PwDs) in all the categories. 
  3.14 The Committee notes that scholarship amount under JRF is Rs 31,000/ - p.m for 2 
years and SRF is Rs 35,000/ - p.m for remaining period. The Commit tee further points out 
that fellowship for Social Science students is Rs10,000 p.a for JRF and Rs20,500/ - p.a for 
SRF and for Science students is Rs 12,000/- p.a for JRF and Rs 25,000/-p.a for SRF.  
3.15 The Committee recommends that t he amount of JRF and SRF should be 
increased to Rs 50,000 p.m to attract bright students for research and innovation  with 
 a  view   to cultivating a proper eco -system for  rigorous research and  creating a pool  
of  highly  qualified  faculty.

measures to address faculty shortages in order to ensure that studies of students are not

05.09.2019 and 22.10.2019 has already issued directions to higher education institutes to fill 
up the vacant posts. 
3.20 The Department informed that for  maintaining  the quality of education, to cover up 
the shortage of teachers, Central Universities   are adopting different methods/process to 
address faculty shortages in order to ensure that studies of students are not affected, which 
inter-alia, include hiring ad -hoc faculty, Guest Faculty, Contract Faculty and Re -
employed.UGC also framed the guidelines for empanelment of Adjunct -Faculty in 
Universities and Colleges. These guidelines enable higher educational institutions to access 
the eminent teachers and researchers  who have completed their formal association with 
University / College, to participate in teaching, to collaborate and to stimulate research 
activities for qualify research at M.Phil. and Ph. D. levels, and to play mentoring and 
inspirational role. Under TEQUIP-III, about 1700 passouts from NIT/ IIT have been engaged 
for 3 years in state technical institutions  of 8 NE states and 11 other states ( Arunachal 
Pradesh, Assam, Himachal Pradesh, Jammu & Kashmir, Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, 
Nagaland, Sikkim, Tripura and Uttarakhand. 
3.21 The Committee has been highlighting the issue of Faculty shortage in Higher 
Education Institutions across the country from time to time . The Committee is anguished  to 
find out that right from Central Universities, IIITs, IITs, NITs, IIMs, IISERs as well as 
Deemed  Universities and Other centrally funded institutions the problem of faculty shortage 
has not been resolved. The Committee points out that more than 35% of posts in teaching are 
vacant in various Higher Education Institutions. The Committee also points out that the 
percentage share of female, SC,ST, OBC and persons with disabilities in various educational 
institutions is very low.  
3.22 The Committee also highlights the fact that the vacancy posts in many of the non -
teaching staff have  also reache d alarming proportion. The Committee points out that more 
than 38% in non -teaching are vacant in various Higher Education Institutions. The 
Committee also highlights this problem has become the biggest impediment for the 
development and growth of  higher education vis a vis maintaining  the quality of education.  

24 
 
3.23 The Committee points out that the main reasons for this  problem not being resolved 
are either the  students are not attracted towards teaching profession or the facilities provided 
at various educational institutions are not of world standard. The Committee also points out 
that many of these Higher Educational Institutions(HEI's) are engaging faculty on contract 
and ad-hoc basis.  
 3.24 The Committee points out that the trend of appointing Adh oc faculty in Higher 
Education Institutions has a potential of creating wrong perceptions about our 
collective commitment to social justice and hence the Department should undertake  
special  recruitment drive to fill these posts within the FY 2021-22. 
 3.25 The Committee  recommends that the Department  should explore the possibility 
of introducing a Common Exam for appointment of faculty and non - faculty for all 
Centrally Funded Educational Institutions by Nat ional Testing Agency (NTA)/UPSC;  
and thereby creating an independent cadre.  
UNIVERSITY GRANTS COMMISSION (UGC) 
3.26 The University Grants Commission (UGC) is a Statutory Body established by an Act 
of Parliament in 1956 for the promotion and coordination of University Education and for the 
determination and maintenance of standards of teaching, examination and research in 
Universities. Apart from providing grants to Universities and colleges, the Commission takes 
measures necessary for development of higher education. The UGC functions from its 
Headquarter at New Delhi and its six Regional Offices located at Hyderabad, Pune, Bhopal, 
Kolkata, Guwahati, Bengaluru and Northern Regional College Bureau in Delhi. 
SCHEME FOR TRANS -DISCIPLINARY RESEARCH FOR INDIA’S DEVELOPING 
ECONOMY (STRIDE) 
3.27 As part of quality mandate, the University Grants Commission (UGC) has also  
launched the Scheme for Trans -Disciplinary Research for India’s Developing Economy 
(STRIDE) on 01.07.19. STRIDE will provide support to the innovative research projects that 
are Soc ially Relevant, Locally Need -based, Nationally Important and Globally Significant. 
The specific focus of the Scheme is to support high impact research in thrust areas of 
humanities and human sciences through networking of experts from institutions and 
organizations across India. The total number of proposals received is 3891. 35 institutions 
were finally selected for Component 1 under STRIDE. 

25 
 
3.28 STRIDE has  the following three components: 
 Component-I:  To develop research culture and interest among young faculty, 
scholars and students to pursue careers and under take the high -quality research in 
trans-disciplinary areas that augment and expand their research capacity. 
 Component-II: To promote trans -disciplinary research and inclusive innovation to 
facilitate national development. 
 Component-III: To conceive, construct, commission, implement and monitor high 
impact innovative projects by identifying best talent to work as a team by creating a 
network of multiple institutions 
3.29 Grant of Accreditation is don e by the National Assessment and Accreditation Council  
(NAAC), an IUC (Inter university Centre )of UGC. The NAAC has identified the following 
set of seven Criteria to serve as the basis of its assessment procedures.  
a) Curricular Aspects 
b) Teaching, Learning and Evaluation 
c) Research, Innovations and Extensions 
d) Infrastructure and Learning Resources 
e) Student Support and Progression 
f) Governance, Leadership and Management 
g) Institutional Values and Best Practices 
 
 3.30 The Committee  recommends that w ith  a view  to  enhancing  employability of 
graduates, UGC should explore the possibility of introducing a two -semester component 
of internship in B.A, B.Com and B.Sc. courses in collaboration with industries/start -ups 
to provide experience based learning and  on the  job  training. 
3.31 The Committee also deliberated on the funds given to various Universities abroad for  
establishment of  Chairs and the number of  scholars from India being  benefited from them. 
3.32 The Committee further recommended that  Ministry should undertake a 
comprehensive evaluation of Chairs set up in foreign universities by the Indian 
organizations through a study group in the FY 2021-22. 
 PANDIT MADAN MOHAN MALAVIYA NATIONAL MISSION ON TEACHERS & 
TEACHING (PMMMNMTT)  
3.33 The Central Sector Scheme of Pandit Madan Mohan Malaviya National Mission on 
Teachers & Teaching (PMMMNMTT) launched in December, 2014. On recommendation of 
the Expenditure Finance Committee (EFC), the Scheme was approved for continuation till 
31st March, 2020. The Scheme PMMMNMTT is proposed for continuation for further five 

26 
 
years for the period 2021 -22 till 2026 -27; which is to be appraised by Standing Finance 
Committee (SFC). Scheme is proposed to be aligned with NEP, 2020.  
3.34 The Department informed the  C ommittee that the  Mission aims at addressing 
comprehensively all issues related to teachers, teaching, teacher preparation, professional 
development, curriculum design, and developing assessment & evaluation methodology, 
research in developing effe ctive Pedagogy. The Mission also has  the  objectives of capacity 
building and  enhancing the quality of faculty in Higher Education  and address specific 
training gaps of school education also, by varied types and forms of training, continuous 
professional development and development of teaching and learning resources. 
3.35 The Mission addresses, on one hand, current and urgent issues such as supply of 
qualified teachers, attracting talent into teaching profession and raising the quality of teaching 
in schools and  colleges. On the other hand, the Mission will pursue long term goals of 
building a strong professional cadre of teachers by setting performance standards and creating 
top class institutional facilities for innovative teaching and professional development of 
teachers. 
3.36 The Department further  elaborated that  thrust of the scheme has been to improve 
quality of teachers & teaching in school and higher education by providing both high quality 
pre-service teacher education programmes and in -service training through capacity building 
and continuous professional development programmes, ICT based pedagogy and specialized 
research in teacher education. Activities have been conducted under non -recurring (new 
building, studio, smart class, ICT lab, training hall, renovation, offset printer, cameras, 
computer, books and furniture) and recurring (training, seminar, workshop, conference, e -
content, offline content, kits, softwares and applications). 
3.37 The Committee recommends that more  teachers training institutes like Pandit 
Madan Mohan Malviya National Mission on Teachers and Teaching (PMMMNTT) be 
created to cater to teacher training in higher education institutions.

I, the Chairman of the Department -related Parliamentary Standing Committee on

2. Consequent upon the re -naming of the Ministry of Human Resource Development as the 
Ministry of Education by amending the Government of India (Allocation o f Business) Rules, 1961
