Recommendation 
1. The Committee recommends that more schools should be opened in hilly Northern region 
States/ North -Eastern States/UTs where there are terrain/resource related difficulties which 
prevent children to take admission in schools.                    (Para: 3.1.10) 
Action Taken 
The Department of School Education and Literacy in its Action Taken Notes informed the 
Committee that education is in the Concurrent List of the Constitution and majority of the schools 
come under the jurisdiction of respective State/ UT Governments - which are the appropriate 
Government under the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education (RTE) Act, 2009. It 
was also informed that in pursua nce to Section 6 of the RTE Act, the Central RTE Rules had 
notified the area or limits of neighbourhood as one kilometre, within which a primary school and 3 
kilometre within which an upper primary school, has to be established. The States have notified 
area or limits of their neighbourhood norms in their state RTE Rules, factoring in their State 
specific condition, for opening of schools. However, under the Act, it is not mandatory for parents 
to send their children only to the neighbourhood schools. State s may give some preference to 
children within a defined distance. 
 
 For providing universal access to quality secondary education, the neighbourhood norms 
notified by the State/UT are applicable for opening of new Secondary Schools. In the case of the 
States and Union Territories, which have not notified the neighbourhood norms for Secondary 
Schools, Samagra Shiksha provides support for access to secondary schools within a distance of 5 
Km and senior secondary schools within 7 -10 Km of a habitation while en suring their viability 
and cost effectiveness.  As reported by States/UTs in their respective Annual Work Plan and 
Budget, in 2021-22, 97.49% and 97.01% of habitations in the country are covered by Primary and 

3 
 
Upper Primary Schools respectively. Also, 95.4 8% and 90.55% of habitations in the country are 
covered by Secondary and Senior Secondary Schools respectively. 
 
 It was also informed that the habitations that remain uncovered are mostly small or 
sparsely populated in difficult areas where opening of sch ool is not feasible for which there is a 
provision of giving transport and escort facility. The Central Government, through integrated 
centrally sponsored scheme of Samagra Shiksha provides support to the States and UTs for 
opening/ strengthening of school s by giving priority for opening of schools in aspirational 
districts, SC, ST, Minority, LWE Affected Districts and Educationally Backward Blocks along 
with relaxation in national norms for hilly region and North Eastern States. With regard to North

Secondary Schools within a distance of 5km and 76.52% of villages were covered by the Higher

Recommendation 
2.  The Committee recommends that the Department should impress upon the Ministry of 
Finance to allocate more funds for the education of SC/ST/Girl/PWDs/Transgender children to 
ensure that the schemes being operated for their upliftment and welfare do not have to face 
resource crunch. The Committee also recommends that the Department should conduct a survey 
to identify the districts where the dropout rates of SC, ST and Girl children are higher than the 
national average. Based upon the findings, an intervention plan should be chalked out no t only to 
bring back these dropout children to school but also to provide them vocational education to 
ensure enhancement in their livelihood abilities, their greater employability and financial 
independence as well as stability.            (Para: 3.1.12) 
Action Taken 
The Department in its written reply informed the Committee that Samagra Shiksha is an 
overarching programme for the school education sector extending from pre -school to class 12 and 
has been prepared with the broader goal of improving school e ffectiveness measured in terms of 
equal opportunities for schooling and equitable learning outcomes , including for 
SC/ST/Girl/PWDs/Transgender children. Under the Samagra Shiksha scheme, Annual Work Plan 
and Budget (AWP&B) Proposals are prepared by each State/UT based on their requirements and 
priority. During the appraisal of AWP&B proposals, all States and UTs are requested to conduct 
household survey an nually for the purpose of identification of Out of School Children (OoSC). 
This includes dropout children and never enrolled. The identified OoSC are brought back to 
school and assessed for their learning gaps. In order to provide universal access of educa tion to all 

7 
 
the children, financial assistance is provided to all States and UTs under Management Monitoring 
Media Evaluation and Research (MMMER) component of the scheme of Samagra Shiksha. 
 
It was also informed that special training for age appropriate a dmission of out of school 
children and residential as well as non -residential training for older children, seasonal hostels / 
residential camps, special training centres at worksites, transport/ escort facility are also supported 
to bring out of school chi ldren to the formal schooling system. Under the student oriented 
component for the children with special needs, financial assistance is provided for identification 
and assessment of children with special needs, aids and appliances, braille kits and books, 
appropriate teaching learning material and stipend to girl students with disability, etc. 
 
The Committee was apprised of the fact that the Department has also developed an online 
module for compiling the data of OoSC identified by each State/UT and their m apping with 
Special Training Centres (STC) on the PRABANDH Portal (http://samagrashiksha.in). The 
concerned State/UT validates the child wise information of the identified OoSC and STC 
uploaded by the concerned Block Resource Centre of the State for monito ring the progress of 
mainstreaming of OoSC. For the first time in 2021 -22, financial assistance upto Rs. 2000 per 
annum has been envisioned for supporting Out of School Children of age group of 16 -19 years, 
belonging to socio economically disadvantaged gro ups, for completing their education through 
NIOS/SIOS, for accessing course materials and certification.  
 
The Department of School Education and Literacy is implementing the scheme of 
Vocationalisation of School Education under the umbrella of ‘Samagra Sh iksha’. The scheme 
aims at integrating Vocational Education with general academic education in all Secondary/Senior 
Secondary schools; enhancing the employability and entrepreneurial abilities of the students, 
providing exposure to work environment; and ge nerating awareness amongst students about 
various career options so as to enable them to make a choice in accordance with their aptitude, 
competence and aspirations. The implementation of Vocational Education has expanded almost 15 
fold in the last eight years, from only 960 schools across 13 states /UTs in 2014 -15 to 14435 
schools across 36 states/UTs in 2021 -22. Currently more than 15 lakh students are undergoing 
Vocational Education under Samagra  Shiksha. Vocational Education has been introduced in 6316 
upper-primary schools all over the country  .The provision for Hub and Spoke Model h as been 
introduced, under which  the infrastructure available in the Hub schools will be utilised by the 

8 
 
students of nearby schools (spoke schools) for vocational training.  ITIs, Polytechnics etc. may 
also be used as hubs.  Under the  Hub & Spoke  model initiated from the year 2021, 139 Hub 
schools and 241 Spoke schools have been approved for the year 2021-22.  
It has been informed that Table 5.13 of the UDISE + 2020 -21 report gives Dropout Rate 
by level of education and gender and can be seen at 
https://udiseplus.gov.in/assets/img/dcf2021/UDISE+2020_21_Booklet_English.pdf  
The Ministr y of Health and Family Welfare has released The National Family Health

assistance will also be provided to concerned States/UTs for onboarding out of school children. 
Recommendation 
3. The Committee recommends that an evaluation study to record the progress and funding 
pattern o f all the Kasturba Gandhi Balika Vidyalayas (KGBVs) should be carried out and a

Recommendation 
4. A Study Group be appointed to review the existing State of Education for Children with 
learning disabilities such as dyslexia, slow learning, autism etc. This study should serve as basis 
for a Policy on this issue.            (Para: 3.1.19) 
Action Taken 
The Department in its written reply informed the Committee that NCERT has been 
requested to form a study group to review the existing state of education for Children with 
learning disabilities such as dyslexia, slow learning, autism etc. and address the issu e of 
identification of SLDs and early interventions across the school system. The study group may 
comprise of representatives from DePWD, RCI, NCTE, NIOS, CBSE and other stakeholders as 
deemed fit. The study would further serve as a basis for a policy on the issue. 
NCERT has initiated following action in the matter: - 
 A study titled “Learning Outcomes of Children with Disabilities: Exploring the Determinants 
in Inclusive Classroom” was conducted during 2020 -21by Regional Institute of Education, 

11 
 
Ajmer with o bjectives to find out the teaching learning determinants of children with 
disabilities in Inclusive setting and t o explore the existing pedagogical processes and 
classroom climate leading to learning outcome in Inclusive setting at primary level 
(Annexure-I). 
 Another study titled “A study of Children with Learning Difficulties and Support Systems 
available in the Elementary Schools of Nagaland” was conducted in Northeast Regional 
Institute of Education, Umiam during 2018 -19 with objectives to ident ify the children with 
learning difficulties in the elementary schools of Nagaland, to study the enabling factors 
available for children with Learning Difficulties and to study the support systems available for 
children with learning difficulties. Brief report is enclosed at Annexure-II 
 Another review of studies titled “Research in Education of Children with Disabilities” was 
conducted in Regional Institute of Education, Bhubneshwar. The softcopy of the paper is 
available on NCERT website. The review present s a systematic and comprehensive 
framework concerning the state of research in the field of education of children with 
disability/disabilities (CwD/CwDs) from the year 2000 to 2017, with a view to identify the key 
areas and generate questions for future re search. Published studies, doctoral dissertations and 
institutional research were considered for mapping the current status. The analysis indicates 
that the area of study is expanding reflecting tremendous growth, research percolating various 
aspects of disability with a focus on empowering them through education. The time following 
the global flagship of Education for All (EFA) with a rights based approach for disability has 
made significant contribution to expansion of research ideas and scope. However, t he analysis 
also shows that the research still seems to be considering disability as a deficit, and the need 
for shifting the focus to capacity approach by magnifying personal capabilities and dignity of 
CwD was felt.  
 NCERT has developed A Teacher’s Handb ook titled ‘Including Children with Autism in 
Primary Classrooms’ which has been published in the year 2019. The handbook was 
developed with the objective to tackle existing issues and spread awareness about autism 
among regular schools teachers, parents and other stakeholders in education.

PRADHAN MANTRI POSHAN SHAKTI NIRMAN (PM POSHAN) SCHEME 
Recommendation 
8. The Committee observes that in the financial year 2021 -22 (till 31.01.2022), only Rs 
6,660.54 crores have been utilized under PM -POSHAN Scheme from the allocated Rs 11,500 
crores which is around 57.91%. It is also understood that not much of the underutilization of 
funds would have been covered in the remaining two months. The Committee al so observes that in 
the year 2020 -21, even though no advertisement & publicity activities under the scheme were 
carried out due to COVID -19 Pandemic, the Department was able to spent 99.87% of the 
allocated funds. Thus, underutilization in such a Welfare S cheme and that too for students 
remains unacceptable. The Committee also takes note of the statement by the Department that 
“there has been no change in funding pattern of the scheme during the COVID -19 pandemic”. 
The Committee therefore, recommends that t here is an urgent need to put in place effective 
strategies for utilizing the funds. Also, it would be prudent on part of the Department to chalk out 
alternative mechanisms if it comes to notice that the implementation and utilization under the 
Scheme is lagging in any quarter so that course correction could be done.                  (Para: 3.2.5) 
 
 

31 
 
Action Taken 
The Committee was informed that BE for PM POSHAN Scheme for the year 2021 -22 is 
Rs 11500 crore which has been reduced to 10233.75 crore at the RE stage as per the outlay 
appraised by Expenditure Finance Committee ( EFC) and approved by Cabinet Committee on 
Economic Affairs (CCEA) . The total allocated fund as RE for the year 2021 -22 i.e. Rs.10233.75 
crore has been utilized during the year 2021-22. 
Recommendation 
9. The Committee is of the view that such a Scheme has the potential to have 
intergenerational effects on child nutrition through improving the mother’s health and education 
levels. Thus, for greater impact and fulfilment of its objectives, reforms towards improving meal 
quality, creating better infrastructure and putting in place stronger systems f or accountability and 
monitoring are a prerequisite. The Committee also notes that with the closure of Schools due to 
the pandemic, household food security has also been affected. Hence, there is a need to take a 
close look at the Scheme so that the existi ng gaps in the scheme can be plugged. There have been 
suggestions for including eggs at least twice a week, introducing a breakfast, extending the school 
meals to include children up to class 10 and enhancing the payments for cooks and helpers. The 
Committee recommends that these suggestions be examined in coordination with experts in the 
field and from the perspective of being beneficial in advancing the objectives, so that required 
action can be taken.              (Para: 3.2.7)  
Action Taken 
The Department in its written replies informed the Committee that during the COVID -19 
pandemic, since schools were closed for major part of the academic year, all enrolled children are 
given Food Security Allowance comprising of food grains and cooking cost in the for m of dry 
ration or cooking cost as Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) under NFSA, 2013 by States and UTs 
during 2020-21 and 2021-22 under PM POSHAN Scheme.  
 
It was further commented that the Department of School Education and Literacy has 
examined inclusion of the new components, inter alia, 'Provision of Breakfast to pre -primary and 
elementary classes', and revision of honorarium to Cook -Cum-Helpers in consultation with the 
Ministry of Finance. However, the Ministry of Finance did not recommend the newly propo sed 
component of Breakfast as well as revision of honorarium to Cook -Cum-Helpers. It may be noted 

32 
 
that the overall responsibilities for providing cooked and nutritious hot cooked meal to the eligible 
children lies with the State Governments and Union Terri tory Administrations in accordance with 
the Guidelines laid down by the Central Government.  The States and UTs fix their menu 
according to their local needs, in order to meet the nutritional content as prescribed in the 
Schedule II of National Food Securi ty Act, 2013.  Some States and UTs provide eggs etc. as 
additional item from their own resources. NFSA, 2013 provides for Hot Cooked Meals upto class 
VIII. However, as States and UTs are free to provide mea ls to students of up to class X also, some 
States and UTs do provide meals to students of classes IX and X also from their own resources.

women, of marginalized groups and first generation learners and qualified candidates of Basic 
Education Literacy Assessment of NLMA.

Learning Outcomes of Children with Disabilities: 
Exploring the Determinants in Inclusive Classroom 
 
Abstract 
 
      The objectives of this project were to find out the teaching learning 
determinants of children with disabilities in Inclusive setting and to explore the 
existing classroom climate of Inclusive school at elementary level. 
In this descriptive research, purposive sampling technique was used for 
selection of sample. 32 CWSNs were selected from different Special schools of 
Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh.  
  A tool on Learning Outcomes for CWSNs was developed by Project 
Investigators. The items were presented under three domains- Language, 
Mathematics, and Environmental Studies. A workshop was conducted for two 
days and experts from the special education and general education with 
expertise in the field of learning outcomes were invited for their guidance on 
developed tool and methods of data collection.  
                   The finally developed tool and the data recording sheet had four 
sections/columns to be completed by the professionals, who were engaged in 
collecting the data.  The data was collected from two schools of Rajasthan and 
two schools of Uttar Pradesh. The collected data (descriptions for each activity) 
was verified by three professionals working in the field of Inclusive/Special 
education.  
The qualitative descriptions were further analyzed and presented in 
deatail    . After obtaining quantitative data, with the help of SPSS, One way 
ANOVA and t test was conducted. It was found that the difference in total 
mean scores of CWSNs studying in Special and Inclusive schools is found 
statistically non-significant. It was also investigated that the difference in 
mean scores achieved by the various groups is although not significant in 
language and environmental science but it is significant in mathematics. 
Further, the performance of children with HI is far better than children with ID, 
and the difference in mean scores of these two groups is highly significant. It 
is also found that gender of CWSNs is does not make significant difference in 
their performance; however the locality of their school and the age group they 
belong is a significant criteria which makes the difference in their learning 
outcome of children with special needs at Primary level.   There were 
difference in responses in the different types of disabilities observed against various stimuli 
and hence the preferred stimuli must be considered for particular group of children with 
special needs. 
 

2 
 
 
 
 
The findings of the study are as follows: 
  It is investigated that the difference between the total mean scores of CWSNs 
studying in Special and Inclusive schools is statistically non-significant 
however the mean scores of CWSNs studying in Inclusive schools are 
comparatively better than the mean scores of CWSNs studying in Special 
schools in all the three domains of learning outcome checklist. Hence the role 
of inclusive education for CWSNs needs to be considered significantly in 
present scenario. 
 The performance of the children belonging to three different groups 
(VI/HI/ID) varies significantly in Mathematics compare to other two subjects 
(Language and EVS). 
 Further the performance of children with Hearing Impairment is 
comparatively very high than performance of children with ID especially in 
mathematics. The mean score shows great variation in abilities in different 
subject/areas within the group of children with Intellectual Disabilities, which 
itself explain the great challenge in front of the inclusive/special teacher for 
the successful Inclusion of children with ID at primary level. 
 When the mean score of the CWSNs from the two different states is 
compared, it is found that the mean scores of the CWSNs from Rajasthan is 
comparatively better than Uttarpradesh and Researcher identified three 
important reasons of achieving comparatively low scores by CWSNs from 
Uttarpradesh-(a) The mean age of CWSNs belong to Rajasthan is 9.6yrs, 
however the mean age of CWSNs from U.P. is 9.3yrs. (b) The number of 
special school from Rajasthan was 20 but the number of special school from 
U.P. is 23 and it was found that the combined total mean score of CWSNs 
from Special school is comparatively poor than the CWSNs from Inclusive 
school and (c) availability of children with ID with comparatively low 
IQ/higher level of retardation from the Uttarpradesh among the selected 
samples. 

3 
 
 It is concluded that gender of CWSNs is does not make significant difference 
in their performance; however the locality of their school may bring 
difference in their performance in functional academics. 
 It is concluded that like children without disability, age is a significant criteria 
which makes the difference in their performance of children with special 
needs.   
 There were difference in responses in the different types of disabilities 
observed against various stimuli and hence the preferred stimuli must be 
considered for particular group of children with special needs.  
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

INTRODUCTION
ln the year 2006 National focus group on education of children with special
needs (NCERT) discusses the issues relating to the provisions, practices and curricular
concerns for children with Special Educational Needs. They recommended making all
schools inclusive by reviewing barriers created by admission procedures (screening,
identification, parental interaction, selection and evaluation), this should include private
schools; buildingthecapacityofteacherstofunctioninaninclusivesetting;makingthe
curriculum flexible and appropriate to accommodate the diversity of school children
including those with disability in both cognitive and non-cognitive areas; making support
services available in the form of technology {including ICT), teaching-learning materials
and specialists; involving parents, family, and the community at all stages of education
ln the year 2AO2, Jha M.M. quoted that barriers to access and success can be
viewed in physical as well as structural sense. But more than that, it is the curriculum,
the pedagogy, the examination and the school's approach, which create barriers. Unless
these unseen barriers are taken care of, access to all children and an assurance of
success to all would remain a far cry. The inclusive education movement, combined with
technological development and a new approach to open schooling has come at this
crucial juncture. Countries 4nd school systems choosing a holistic approach to access
and success are more likely to succeed in reaching educltion for all.
For the present study Learning difficulties refer to the learners who are facing
problems in reading, writing and math which are not because of other kind of disability
like visual, hearing and physical impairment.
During SCC Meetin g 2017 it was raising un irrr" regarding the need of
identification of students with learning difficulties in the elementary schools of
Nagaland. Only the identification of these children may not help us to plan and provide
corrective measures. Therefore, it was proposed to study about the state of learning
difficulties and support systems available in the elementary schools of Nagaland.

RESEARCH QUESTIONS
1. What is the state of students with Learning Difficulties in the elementary
schools of Nagaland?
2. What are the support systems available for children with Learning Difficulties
in the elementary schools of Nagaland'
PROCESS
A quantitative approach was adopted for answering to the research questions.
Participants of the study students with learning difficulties {SwLD} from elementary
schools of Nagaland. Their identity is not disclosed instead numeric code was assigned.
They were identified by gender, grade level and school administrator. The purpose of
the study was to identify children with learning difficulties and support systems available
at elementary schools of Nagaland.
Two digital based checklists were developed, these are to fill by class teachers
and school authority.
Firstly, Proforma A: Checklist for identifliing children with learning difficulties in
elementary schools, is the one which needs to bd filled by the class teacher. The purpose
of this checklist is to identify the difficulties and its level facing by SwLD in elementary
school. The checklist consists five domains viz. language skills, reading skills, writing
skills, math skills and attention and 83 items (13 for language, L6 for reading, 2A for
writing, 23 for math and tL for attention), also it has a provision for giving other
observation and information they want to share. Five rating scale system was followed
in this proforma viz. always, frequently, sometimes, never and not noticed.
Secondly, Proforma B: Checklist for identifliing support systems fbr educating
children with learning difficulties in elementary schools. The purpose of the checklist is
to collect information on basic requirements for providing services for SwLD in
